hints: Think about what phases the ester, water and dilute acid are in during this hydrolysis.
Recall the definition that links same phase to homogeneous catalysis and different phase to heterogeneous catalysis.
Remember what is always true of any catalyst about being regenerated and lowering activation energy, then pick the statement that fits.
walkthrough:
**Picture the reaction mixture**

Think of ester hydrolysis with dilute acid. The ester, water and $H^+$ ions from the acid are all mixed together in one aqueous solution.

$$\text{ester (aq) + water (l) } \xrightarrow{H^+(aq)} \text{ carboxylic acid + alcohol}$$

**Apply homogeneous vs heterogeneous**

A catalyst in the same physical state or phase as the reactants is homogeneous. A catalyst in a different phase is heterogeneous.

Here $H^+(aq)$ is in the same aqueous phase as the reactants, so this is homogeneous catalysis.

**Check catalyst rules**

A great catalyst is never used up, it is regenerated at the end. It also always works by providing an alternative route of lower activation energy, $E_a$.

options.A: Incorrect. Heterogeneous means catalyst and reactants are in different phases, e.g. solid iron with gaseous nitrogen and hydrogen. Here $H^+$ is dissolved in the same solution as the ester and water, so it is homogeneous, not heterogeneous.
options.B: Correct. In acid hydrolysis the $H^+$ ions, ester and water are all in the same aqueous phase. A catalyst in the same phase as reactants is defined as a homogeneous catalyst.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the classic catalyst trap. $H^+$ ions take part in the mechanism by protonating the ester, but they are regenerated at the end, so there is no overall consumption.
options.D: Incorrect. All catalysts, including $H^+$, speed up reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. They have no effect on overall enthalpy change, but they definitely lower $E_a$.
